column4: The exact designation أَصْحَابُ ٱلْمَيْمَنَةِ reappears as one of the judgment-day classes, directly staging the section's right-hand people.
The exact opposing designation أَصْحَابُ ٱلْمَشْـَٔمَةِ makes the left-hand class the spatial and fateful counterpart of 56:8.
Judgment makes humanity أَزْوَاجًا ثَلَاثَةً, explicitly turning lived differences into fixed classes; 56:8-10 name those three classes.
أَصْحَابُ ٱلْيَمِينِ restates the right-hand people with the hand-name which the section identifies as an alternative to meymene.
أَصْحَابُ ٱلشِّمَالِ restates the adverse class with the literal left-hand name and begins its contrasting fate.
The record is physically given بِيَمِينِهِۦ, making the right side a disclosed judgment outcome rather than merely a direction.
The record given بِشِمَالِهِۦ makes the left side the place of irreversible regret and directly opposes 69:19.
Receiving the record بِيَمِينِهِۦ identifies the fortunate side at the moment of reckoning.
Receiving the record وَرَآءَ ظَهْرِهِۦ is a deliberate alternative staging of the adverse side, contrasted with the right-hand reception in 84:7.
إِلَّآ أَصْحَابَ ٱلْيَمِينِ exempts the right-hand people from the universal pledge for deeds stated in 74:38.
Believers' light running before them and بِأَيْمَانِهِمْ gives the right side visible radiance on the day their destination is announced.
Believers recall light moving before them and بِأَيْمَانِهِمْ while asking God to perfect it, repeating the luminous right-side scene as prayer.
People are summoned by their leaders and the one given a record بِيَمِينِهِۦ can read it without injustice, another direct right-hand judgment scene.
The two receivers seated عَنِ ٱلْيَمِينِ وَعَنِ ٱلشِّمَالِ turn right and left into the enduring positions from which a life is recorded.
The sun's movement ذَاتَ ٱلْيَمِينِ and ذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِ makes the two words a literal spatial arrangement around the protected cave.
The sleepers are turned ذَاتَ ٱلْيَمِينِ وَذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِ, a bodily right-left scene that continues 18:17.
Two gardens عَن يَمِينٍ وَشِمَالٍ flank Saba's dwelling, and both belong to a blessed provision scene, complicating any automatic equation of physical left with ill fortune.
The call comes from شَاطِئِ ٱلْوَادِ ٱلْأَيْمَنِ in ٱلْبُقْعَةِ ٱلْمُبَارَكَةِ, explicitly joining the right side to blessing, the section's dictionary sense of yumn.
God calls Moses مِن جَانِبِ ٱلطُّورِ ٱلْأَيْمَنِ and draws him near, making the right side a site of divine nearness.
The covenant at جَانِبَ ٱلطُّورِ ٱلْأَيْمَنَ is immediately joined to the gift of manna and quails, linking the right side with provision and favor.
Created things cast their shadows عَنِ ٱلْيَمِينِ وَٱلشَّمَآئِلِ while prostrating, so both physical sides share submission rather than bearing opposed moral fates.
Satan threatens approach from before, behind, عَنْ أَيْمَانِهِمْ and عَن شَمَآئِلِهِمْ; here both sides are avenues of trial, setting a boundary on the final moral labels.
The rejecters cluster عَنِ ٱلْيَمِينِ وَعَنِ ٱلشِّمَالِ around the messenger, showing that occupying either physical side does not itself make one of the fortunate companions.
What Moses holds فِى يَمِينِكَ swallows the magicians' craft; the right hand becomes effective power, matching the section's dictionary statement اليمين القوة.
Abraham strikes the idols ضَرْبًۢا بِٱلْيَمِينِ; the right hand is the instrument of decisive force and directly realizes the named strength sense.
The heavens are مَطْوِيَّاتٌۢ بِيَمِينِهِۦ, using the right hand in a scene of absolute divine power and scale.
لَأَخَذْنَا مِنْهُ بِٱلْيَمِينِ uses yamin in a seizure of power, a direct Qur'anic setting for the section's secondary definition of right hand as strength.
لِّأَصْحَابِ ٱلْيَمِينِ identifies the whole garden description in 56:28-37 as the prepared lot of the right-hand people.
At the deathbed classification, being مِنْ أَصْحَابِ ٱلْيَمِينِ makes the right-hand identity the soul's final disclosed station.
سَلَامٌۭ لَّكَ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ ٱلْيَمِينِ gives the right-hand class a greeting of peace, supplying the felicity implicit in the section's yumn.
وَٱلسَّابِقُونَ ٱلسَّابِقُونَ names the third class required by 56:7, preventing the right-left pair from erasing the foremost group in this particular judgment scene.
أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ ٱلْمُقَرَّبُونَ states the distinctive outcome of the third class named in 56:10.
Thornless lote trees begin the concrete dwelling of the right-hand people named in 56:27 and completed by 56:38.
Layered fruit continues the provision assigned to the right-hand people, making their side a lived felicity.
Extended shade contributes a lasting place of rest to the right-hand group's destination.
Flowing water continues the right-hand people's promised setting and its association with blessing.
Abundant fruit supplies another concrete feature of the right-hand side's provision.
Fruit that is neither cut off nor forbidden makes the right-hand fortune continuous rather than passing.
Raised couches give the right-hand group a settled place, realizing the section's claim that a chosen direction becomes an abiding location.
A renewed creation continues the right-hand people's garden scene and specifies the felicity attached to their class.
The companions' renewed virginity belongs to the same sustained description of the right-hand destination.
Loving, equal-aged companions finish the immediate description before 56:38 assigns it to أَصْحَابِ ٱلْيَمِينِ.
A multitude from earlier peoples is included within the right-hand class, showing that the side gathers a transhistorical company.
A multitude from later peoples completes the temporal breadth of that same right-hand company.
Scorching wind and boiling water begin the concrete fate attached to the left-hand people named in 56:41.
The shade of black smoke turns the left-hand side into an adverse dwelling rather than mere direction.
The left-hand shade is neither cool nor pleasant, directly reversing the extended shade of the right-hand scene in 56:30.
Former indulgence explains a lived choice that hardened into membership among the left-hand people.
Persistence in the great sin supplies the moral adherence behind their adverse side, complementing the section's definition of ṣāḥib as one who stays attached.
Their denial that death will be followed by resurrection voices the stance that leads into the left-hand outcome.
Their question about resurrected ancestors completes the disbelief spoken in 56:47.
The command to say that earlier and later peoples will all be gathered answers the left-hand group's denial.
Gathering at a fixed time turns the moral division into an appointed judgment event.
Eating from the tree of zaqqum begins the left-hand group's humiliating reception.
Filling their bellies with zaqqum intensifies the adverse provision assigned to that side.
Drinking boiling water answers the garden's flowing water with the left-hand side's opposite provision.
Drinking like thirsty camels completes that punitive meal scene.
هَـٰذَا نُزُلُهُمْ يَوْمَ ٱلدِّينِ names the preceding food and drink as the left-hand group's judgment-day hospitality.

The soul reaching the throat opens the death scene that soon sorts it among the near, the right-hand people, or the denying lost; it also meets the source dictionary's death-and-right-side burial sense.
The dying person's first possible class is one of those brought near, retaining the threefold division introduced in 56:7-11.
Rest, fragrant provision, and a garden state the outcome of the near class before the right-hand class is named.
The alternative وَأَمَّآ إِن كَانَ مِنَ ٱلْمُكَذِّبِينَ ٱلضَّآلِّينَ introduces the adverse class by its denial and wandering.
Boiling-water hospitality gives that denying class its concrete reception.
Burning in Hell completes the adverse destination opposed to the peace of the right-hand people in 56:91.
The right-hand recipient says he expected to meet his account, explicitly opposing the mistaken حساب of the human in 90:5 and 90:7.
فَهُوَ فِى عِيشَةٍۢ رَّاضِيَةٍۢ turns receipt on the right into a satisfying settled life.
A lofty garden supplies the lasting place attached to the right-hand judgment.
Near-hanging fruit specifies the accessible provision of that fortunate side.
The invitation to eat and drink for deeds sent ahead ties the right-hand outcome to prior action on the path.
The left-hand recipient wishes never to have known his account, reversing the confidence of 69:20.
His wish that death had been final shows the irreversible misery disclosed by the left-hand record.
مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ rejects accumulated wealth as a power able to change the left-hand outcome.
هَلَكَ عَنِّى سُلْطَـٰنِيَهْ declares worldly authority gone, sharply limiting the dictionary association of the right hand with human power.
The order to seize and shackle the left-hand recipient begins the execution of his adverse place.
Casting him into Hell makes the left-side verdict an actual destination.
Binding him in a long chain makes his attachment to that destination bodily and inescapable.
Failure to believe in God names the first path choice behind the left-hand fate, matching 90:19's disbelief in God's signs.
Failure to urge feeding the needy directly reverses 90:14-16 and explains why this person receives the left-hand record.
Having no intimate friend that day gives a grim interpersonal counterpoint to aṣḥāb as an enduring company.
The only food being foul discharge continues the left-hand side's reversed provision.
Only sinners eat that food, closing the explanation of who belongs to this adverse company.
A lenient reckoning is the first consequence of receiving the record on the right.
Returning joyfully to one's people turns right-hand reception into reunion and felicity.
The behind-the-back recipient calls for destruction, voicing the adverse verdict corresponding to the left side.
Entering a blaze makes the alternative book-reception an enduring location.
His former delight among his people supplies the earthly stance behind the adverse end and reverses 84:9's rightful joy.
He supposed he would never return, identifying the false expectation behind his judgment-side placement.
بَلَىٰٓ إِنَّ رَبَّهُۥ كَانَ بِهِۦ بَصِيرًۭا answers that supposition with the divine seeing also stressed in 90:7.
Every soul is pledged for what it earned; 74:39 then marks the right-hand people as the exception, grounding side in deed.
The right-hand people are فِى جَنَّـٰتٍۢ, giving their class a settled garden location.
They question the criminals from within the gardens, staging communication across the two destinations.
مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِى سَقَرَ asks what course put the criminals into Saqar, directly joining way taken to final place.
The criminals first answer that they were not among those who prayed, naming one practice behind their opposing destination.
Their admission that they did not feed the needy directly reverses 90:14-16 and explains exclusion from the right-hand people.
Joining vain discourse names the company and conduct in which they remained attached.
Their denial of the Day of Judgment matches the disbelief in signs that defines 90:19's adverse group.
Certainty arriving ends their denial and fixes the consequence narrated by the whole exchange.
Hypocrites ask believers to share their light, but a wall divides mercy on its inner side from punishment outside, spatializing the final separation.
The exchange across the wall names self-temptation, waiting, doubt, and false hopes as the path that left the hypocrites without light.
No ransom is accepted and the Fire becomes their refuge, making the wall's separation permanent.
On the coming day humanity is divided فَمِنْهُمْ شَقِىٌّۭ وَسَعِيدٌۭ, an exact nonlexical counterpart to ill-fated and fortunate sides.
Those made wretched are placed in the Fire, giving the adverse fortune of 11:105 a destination.
Their abiding in the Fire makes the adverse class's side enduring rather than momentary.
Those made happy abide in the Garden, directly realizing the section's equation of the fortunate side with lasting felicity.
فَرِيقٌۭ فِى ٱلْجَنَّةِ وَفَرِيقٌۭ فِى ٱلسَّعِيرِ states the same final spatial division into two enduring companies without right-left vocabulary.
The verse directly opposes أَصْحَابُ ٱلنَّارِ and أَصْحَابُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ and declares the Garden's companions successful, exposing ṣāḥib as attachment to a fate.
A sin that encloses its doer leads to أَصْحَابُ ٱلنَّارِ who remain there, a direct adverse counterpart to the section's enduring side-membership.
Belief and good deeds lead to أَصْحَابُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ who remain there, the paired fortunate company after 2:81.
Believers who do good are named أَصْحَابُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ and remain there, directly combining company, place, and permanence.
The Garden company recognizes that guidance brought it to its inherited destination, linking the end-place back to the way.
أَصْحَابُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ call to أَصْحَابَ ٱلنَّارِ across their destinations, explicitly staging the two companies as opposed sides.
Those on the adverse side are identified by blocking God's way and seeking to make it crooked, a direct path-to-place relation.
A barrier stands between the two companies and the people of the Heights recognize both by marks, making their separation a visible spatial order.
When the Heights people's eyes turn toward the Fire's companions, they ask not to be placed with the wrongdoers.
The Heights people address men known by their marks, continuing the recognition of the separated companies.
Those once denied mercy are told to enter the Garden, dramatizing the true allocation against human misjudgment.
The Fire's companions ask the Garden's companions for water or provision, making the opposed sides and their reversed provisions explicit.
The answer explains that denial and treating religion as play barred the Fire's companions from the Garden's provision.
Those who do good become أَصْحَابُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ and abide there, joining conduct, fortunate company, and lasting place.
Those who earn evil become أَصْحَابُ ٱلنَّارِ and abide there, the adjacent adverse company to 10:26.
Belief, good deeds, and humility lead to أَصْحَابُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ who abide there, another direct company fixed to its destination.
مَثَلُ ٱلْفَرِيقَيْنِ compares the two parties as blind/deaf and seeing/hearing, making their difference mutually defining like right and left.
أَصْحَابُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ abide there as repayment for deeds, explicitly grounding enduring company in the path already lived.
Disbelievers are driven in companies to Hell until its gates open, staging one collective route to an adverse permanent place.
The command to enter Hell and abide there closes the disbelieving company's route with permanence.
Those who feared their Lord are driven in companies to the Garden, the opposite procession and destination to 39:71.
The Garden company praises God for granting the land to settle wherever it wills, articulating the end-place as an inherited, abiding side.
يَوْمَئِذٍۢ يَتَفَرَّقُونَ makes the Hour itself the event in which people are separated.
Believers who did good are made joyful in a garden, specifying one side of the separation announced in 30:14.
Those who disbelieved and denied the signs and afterlife are brought to punishment, specifying the other side in terms matching 90:19.
فَمِنكُمْ كَافِرٌۭ وَمِنكُم مُّؤْمِنٌۭ gives the belief-disbelief division that 90:17-19 turns into the two named sides.
On the Day of Gathering, faith and good action lead to forgiveness and abiding gardens, giving one gathered class its destination.
Disbelief and denial of signs lead to أَصْحَابُ ٱلنَّارِ, closely matching the definition of 90:19's left-side people.
إِنَّا هَدَيْنَـٰهُ ٱلسَّبِيلَ إِمَّا شَاكِرًۭا وَإِمَّا كَفُورًا parallels the two guided high roads and immediately divides response into gratitude or disbelief.
Chains and a blaze are prepared for the disbelievers, turning one response to the guided way into an adverse end-place.
The righteous drink a fragrant cup, beginning the opposite provision for those who took the grateful course.
The oath's answer إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّىٰ declares human strivings divergent, the same movement from an opening oath toward separated outcomes.
Giving and being mindful begins the conduct of one of the two divergent courses.
Affirming the best completes the stance that leads to the fortunate course.

فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises facilitation toward ease; the source section's dictionary form yusrā means the left side, so this Qur'anic sense deliberately prevents equating the spelling with ill fortune.
Miserliness and self-sufficiency begin the opposite course and recall the hoarded wealth of 90:6.
Denying the best gives that adverse course the same stance of denial that marks 90:19.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ promises facilitation toward hardship, completing the two opposed trajectories.
Only ٱلْأَشْقَى enters the greatest Fire, giving ill fortune its final place.
وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا ٱلْأَتْقَى places the mindful person away from that Fire, opposing the ill-fated class.
The mindful person gives wealth to purify himself, echoing the costly ascent before membership among 90's right-hand people.
Within an oath sequence, the soul and the One who proportioned it introduce an interior field that will be morally divided.
The soul is inspired with both its wickedness and its mindfulness, a nonspatial pair of possible courses corresponding to the two high roads.
Purifying the soul succeeds, giving one inspired course its fortunate outcome.
Corrupting the soul fails, completing the opposed outcomes after the oath sequence.
The oath by time opens a compact movement from oath to human separation, structurally paralleling surah 90's opening and close.
Humanity is declared in loss before an exception is made, establishing the adverse side of the division.
Faith, good deeds, and mutual counsel to truth and patience define the exception, closely meeting 90:17's faith and mutual counsel before the right-hand designation.

نَحْنُ قَسَمْنَا بَيْنَهُم مَّعِيشَتَهُمْ uses q-s-m for God's distribution of livelihoods, directly realizing the source dictionary's تقسيم/تفريق sense while distinguishing providential allotment from final moral division.
When relatives, orphans, and the needy attend ٱلْقِسْمَةَ, they are to receive provision and kind words; the q-s-m division sense meets the vulnerable people whose care precedes 90's final sorting.
فَٱلْمُقَسِّمَـٰتِ أَمْرًا names those distributing affairs inside an oath sequence, joining both senses developed by the section: oath and apportionment.
ٱلْمُقْتَسِمِينَ names the dividers, a direct q-s-m occurrence whose object is specified in 15:91.
Those dividers make the Qur'an عِضِينَ, fragments; this adverse partition of revelation contrasts with the just separation of people according to response to God's signs.
تِلْكَ إِذًۭا قِسْمَةٌۭ ضِيزَىٰ condemns an unjust division, establishing a moral boundary around the section's q-s-m image of final separation.
Those seeking emancipation from مِمَّا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَـٰنُكُمْ are to receive a contract and God's wealth, joining the right hand's power/possession sense to 90:13's freeing of a neck.

Kindness is commanded toward parents, kin, orphans, the needy, neighbors, traveler, and مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَـٰنُكُمْ; right-hand power is placed under the same mercy ethic that precedes 90's right-hand outcome.

Righteousness is not turning faces east or west but faith, giving to kin, orphans and the needy, freeing people, and patience; it explicitly relocates moral sidedness from direction to the deeds of 90:13-17.

Pharaoh's people claim good as theirs but treat evil as an omen from Moses; the reply locates their طَـٰٓئِرُهُمْ with God, correcting the section's dictionary association of side with good or bad luck.
The people say ٱطَّيَّرْنَا بِكَ to Salih, and he answers that their omen is with God; responsibility replaces their projection of ill fortune onto a messenger.
The town's people say إِنَّا تَطَيَّرْنَا بِكُمْ and threaten the messengers, staging the human attribution of misfortune which the section associates with shu'm.
طَـٰٓئِرُكُم مَّعَكُمْ returns their alleged omen to themselves, turning external bad luck into responsibility for their own excess.

The owners do not make those whom أَيْمَـٰنُهُمْ possess equal partners in provision; it exposes the power and inequality carried by “right hand,” which 90's command to free a neck morally challenges.
The parable asks whether those whom your right hands possess are equal partners in provision; it makes right-hand power a social hierarchy rather than an automatic sign of personal blessedness.
One walking fallen on his face is contrasted with one walking upright عَلَىٰ صِرَٰطٍۢ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ, a direct path-image for two ways whose ends cannot be equal.
قَد تَّبَيَّنَ ٱلرُّشْدُ مِنَ ٱلْغَىِّ explicitly distinguishes right guidance from error before 2:257 gives the two allegiances their opposed ends.
God leads believers from darkness to light, while false powers lead rejecters from light to darkness and make them أَصْحَابُ ٱلنَّارِ, a two-course division ending in adhered company.
The truth is announced and belief or disbelief is left as a response, after which a surrounding Fire is prepared for wrongdoers; choice of course becomes place.
Belief and good deeds receive an unlost reward, supplying the fortunate counterpart to the fire scene in 18:29.
أَفَمَن كَانَ مُؤْمِنًۭا كَمَن كَانَ فَاسِقًۭا declares the two moral classes unequal, the conceptual boundary behind their different destinations.
Believers who do good receive gardens as lodging, placing one class in its prepared home.
The defiantly disobedient have the Fire as lodging and are returned whenever they try to leave, making the adverse side lasting.
هَـٰذَانِ خَصْمَانِ divides people into two adversarial parties concerning their Lord and begins the Fire-side description.
Believers who do good are admitted to gardens, supplying the other party's destination after the adverse scene begun in 22:19.
Disbelievers among the People of the Book and polytheists abide in Hell, the adverse company created by rejection of signs.
Believers who do good are خَيْرُ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ, the explicitly opposed human class.
Their reward is abiding gardens and mutual divine pleasure, giving the believing class its permanent fortunate place.
The messenger neither recited a prior book nor wrote one بِيَمِينِكَ; its book-and-right-hand conjunction forms a specific earthly counter-scene to records received in the right hand at judgment.
God asks Moses what is فِى يَمِينِكَ, presenting the right hand first as ordinary grasp before 20:69 makes what it holds an instrument of power.

The condemned say others used to come عَنِ ٱلْيَمِينِ; whether “from the right” means the trusted side or forceful approach, it is a significant non-felicitous use of the section's side/strength word.
Every spoken word has a ready watcher, stating what the right-and-left receivers of 50:17 actually record.
Inheritors of the Book are divided into self-wronging, moderate, and foremost classes, a threefold moral classification comparable to 56:7 rather than a simple binary.
The speakers divide themselves into submitters and deviators, and say the submitters deliberately sought right guidance.
The deviators become fuel for Hell, turning the class distinction of 72:14 into an adverse destination.
On judgment day some faces whiten and others blacken, giving the human division two visibly opposed conditions and addressing the rejecters for disbelief.
Those with whitened faces remain in God's mercy, completing the fortunate side of the visible division.
Some faces are radiant on that day, beginning one embodied judgment class.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord, specifying the fortunate stance of that class.
Other faces are gloomy on that day, the visible opposite class.
They expect a back-breaking calamity, explaining the ill fortune written on the gloomy faces.
Faces bright on that day give one judgment company a recognizable sign.
Laughter and rejoicing express that company's fortunate state.
Dust-covered faces introduce the opposed judgment company.
Darkness covering those faces deepens the contrast with the bright group.
أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْكَفَرَةُ ٱلْفَجَرَةُ identifies the dark-faced group by disbelief and transgression, matching 90:19's defining stance.
Heavy scales begin a two-outcome judgment based on what was acquired along the way.
A pleasing life is the settled outcome of the heavy-scaled class.
Light scales introduce the opposite measured class.
The abyss becomes that class's destination, turning measured difference into place.
The record of the wicked is in Sijjin, assigning one moral class to a named adverse register.
The question about Sijjin emphasizes that the adverse register is a distinct judgment reality.
A written record defines Sijjin's function and links class placement to inscription.
The record of the righteous is in Illiyyin, the opposed register to Sijjin.
The question about Illiyyin formally mirrors 83:8 and marks the paired registers.
A written record defines the righteous register just as 83:9 defines the wicked one.
Those brought near witness the righteous record, linking this register with the third class named in 56:10-11.
The human mistakes generous provision for divine honor, exposing an unreliable earthly reading of blessing and fortune.
He mistakes measured provision for humiliation, the opposite error about fortune and allotted share.
The correction begins with failure to honor the orphan, moving the criterion from fortune to the deeds on 90's steep path.
Failure to urge feeding the needy repeats the omission that elsewhere explains the adverse judgment side.
ٱلْمَآءَ قِسْمَةٌۢ بَيْنَهُمْ uses q-s-m for a regulated division of water, a concrete temporal allotment distinct from the final division of people.
A destructive wind is sent فِى يَوْمِ نَحْسٍۢ مُّسْتَمِرٍّۢ, a Qur'anic scene of an ill-fated day corresponding to the section's shu'm sense.
أَيَّامٍۢ نَّحِسَاتٍۢ names calamitous days in which the wind makes a people taste disgrace, another concrete expression of ill fortune.
Gardens of delight give the foremost third class named in 56:10-11 its own destination alongside the right- and left-hand classes.
A multitude from earlier peoples belongs to the foremost class, beginning its transhistorical composition.
A smaller number from later peoples completes the composition of the foremost class.
Jeweled couches begin the concrete dwelling of the foremost class, completing the three-class scene introduced in 56:7.
Reclining face to face makes the foremost class a settled company in its destination.
Everlasting youths attending them continues the provision assigned to the foremost class.
Cups and a drink from a flowing spring specify the foremost class's reception.
Their drink causes neither headache nor loss of reason, distinguishing this fortunate provision from harmful drink.
Chosen fruit continues the provision of the foremost class.
Desired bird meat adds to the concrete hospitality of the foremost class.
Wide-eyed companions continue the foremost class's garden scene.
The comparison to hidden pearls describes the companions in that same destination.
The foremost class's provision is explicitly a recompense for what they used to do, tying final place to prior course.
They hear neither vain speech nor sinful talk, distinguishing their lasting company from corrupt association.
Only words of peace are heard, giving the foremost class the greeting later echoed for the right-hand people in 56:91.
The witnesses look on as the soul reaches the throat, contributing the human vantage within the death scene that ends in threefold classification.
God is nearer to the dying person than the onlookers although they cannot see, locating the final sorting under unseen divine presence.
The challenge to those who suppose they will not be judged introduces accountability immediately before the soul's class is disclosed.
The demand to return the departing soul if they are truthful establishes death's irreversibility before the three outcomes are named.
The declaration that the preceding division is certain truth seals the three deathbed outcomes as final reality.
The universal exposure in which no secret remains hidden sets the judgment scene immediately before records are given on the right or left.
Every human labors toward the Lord and will meet Him; the next ayat disclose the two book-reception outcomes of that journey.
Intercession no longer benefits the criminals, confirming the finality of the course into Saqar explained in 74:42-47.
When Saba turns away, the two gardens on right and left are replaced by bitter, sparse gardens, turning bilateral blessing into loss through response.
The replacement is identified as recompense for ingratitude, showing that fortune attached to the two sides changed through moral choice.
Each rejecter clustered on the messenger's right and left hopes to enter a garden, explicitly exposing the difference between physical side and final fortunate side.
The emphatic refusal answers their hope, denying that their physical placement or presumption grants garden membership.
Each person's طَائِرَهُ is fastened to his neck and brought out as an open record, joining fortune or omen, inescapable attachment, and judgment book in one scene.
The person is commanded to read his own record and suffice as his own reckoner, completing the book scene begun by the fastened omen in 17:13.
The trumpet, death, and resurrection gather all people into the judgment event that culminates in the two processions of 39:71 and 39:73.
The earth shines, the record is set down, and witnesses are brought before judgment, directly preparing the two groups' departure to their destinations.
Every soul is fully repaid for what it did immediately before the two companies are driven toward Hell and Garden.
The leaders answer the accusation about approaching from the right by saying their followers were not believers, beginning the ayah-by-ayah clarification of that phrase.
They deny having authority over the followers and call them transgressors, clarifying that “coming from the right” did not remove the followers' responsibility.
Both parties acknowledge that their Lord's word has fallen due and that they will taste punishment, giving the disputed influence its shared destination.
The leaders admit leading others astray because they themselves were astray, explicitly linking companionship to loss of the way.
Leaders and followers share punishment that day, making their chosen association an enduring adverse company.
After the sign cast from Moses's right hand defeats the illusion, the magicians fall prostrate and believe, showing that right-hand power serves guidance.
Whoever turns from the Merciful's remembrance is assigned a satan as an inseparable companion, a concrete adverse form of attachment.
Those companions bar people from the path while the barred people suppose themselves guided, joining companionship directly to a mistaken course.
At the final encounter, the person wishes the distance of the two easts lay between him and his companion, revealing the terrible permanence of the association.
Sharing punishment makes regret useless, turning the attached companionship into common residence on the adverse side.
At judgment the wrongdoer wishes he had taken a path with the messenger, directly presenting final regret over a chosen way.
He wishes he had not taken a particular person as intimate friend, identifying companionship as the fork in that path.
The friend led him away from remembrance after it came, explaining how adhered company produced the adverse end.
Garden inhabitants turn toward one another and ask questions, opening a recollection of a companion who ended on the opposite side.
One Garden inhabitant says he once had a close companion, making personal companionship the hinge of the cross-destination scene.
The former companion had challenged belief in resurrection, voicing the denial that belongs to the adverse course.
He had mocked judgment after death and decay, specifying the belief that separated the two companions.
The Garden speaker asks his company whether they will look, initiating literal sight across the two destinations.
He looks and sees the former companion in the midst of Hell, spatializing the opposed outcomes of their paths.
The Garden speaker says the companion nearly brought him to ruin, naming the causal force of that association.
He credits his Lord's favor for not being among those brought to punishment, locating true good fortune in rescue from the companion's course.
The Garden speaker asks whether they will die again, beginning his recognition that the fortunate destination endures.
He contrasts their first death with freedom from punishment, confirming the permanence of his side.
He names this outcome the great triumph, articulating the felicity attached to his destination.
The call for workers to work toward such an outcome reconnects the final side to action taken before judgment.

أَقْسَمُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ جَهْدَ أَيْمَـٰنِهِم combines q-s-m swearing with aymān as oaths while discussing demanded signs and unbelief, bringing the section's oath, right-root, and signs into one wording.
أَقْسَمُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ جَهْدَ أَيْمَـٰنِهِم again combines the two roots in an oath denying resurrection, the event where the two sides are finally disclosed.
People swear جَهْدَ أَيْمَـٰنِهِم that a warner would make them better guided, yet the warner increases aversion; q-s-m, aymān, and the rejected path meet here.
People أَقْسَمُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ جَهْدَ أَيْمَـٰنِهِم that they would obey, but are told not to swear and instead render known obedience, separating oath-language from actual course.
The prohibition on seeking allotted fortune with divining arrows, تَسْتَقْسِمُوا۟ بِٱلْأَزْلَـٰمِ, joins q-s-m division to attempted fortune and sets a boundary on that practice.
People attribute good fortune to God and misfortune to the messenger, and are told that all is from God, directly correcting human side-like assignments of luck.
Good reaching a person is from God while evil reaching him is from himself, adding moral responsibility to the fortune language of 4:78.
At the descent, God promises that whoever follows His guidance will neither fear nor grieve, giving one response to the offered path its outcome.
Those who disbelieve and deny the signs become abiding أَصْحَابُ ٱلنَّارِ, matching 90:19 and completing the alternative to 2:38.
God promises that whoever follows His guidance will neither stray nor suffer, turning the offered way into one of two life trajectories.
Turning away from remembrance leads to a constricted life and resurrection blind, giving the rejected course its adverse outcome.
The resurrected person asks why he was raised blind after once seeing, voicing the consequence of his chosen course.
The answer says God's signs came and were forgotten, so he is forgotten that day, closely matching the rejection of signs defining 90's left-hand group.
Excess and unbelief receive recompense, and the afterlife punishment is declared more severe and lasting.
God commands following His straight path and forbids the multiple paths that scatter people from it, a direct decision-point image for way becoming side.
God owns direction to the intended way while some ways deviate, explicitly setting guidance and deviation within the road image.
Following a way other than the believers' way after guidance becomes clear ends in Hell, directly joining selected path to final destination.
Every soul tastes death, and true success is being drawn away from Fire and admitted to Garden, compressing death and the two final sides into one ayah.
أَصْحَابَ ٱلْجَنَّةِ are joyfully occupied on judgment day, opening a scene of the fortunate company immediately before criminals are separated.
The Garden company and their spouses recline in shade, giving that company a settled place.
Fruit and whatever they request supply the Garden company's provision.
A word of peace from a merciful Lord crowns the fortunate company's scene.
وَٱمْتَـٰزُوا۟ ٱلْيَوْمَ أَيُّهَا ٱلْمُجْرِمُونَ commands the criminals to separate themselves that day, explicitly forming the opposite company.
The mindful are gathered to the Merciful as an honored delegation, one collective route toward the fortunate destination.
The criminals are driven thirsty toward Hell, the adjacent opposite procession and destination.
God separates the corrupt from the good, heaps the corrupt together, and places them in Hell, making moral distinction into grouped destination.
The question contrasts one cast into Fire with one arriving secure on judgment day, a concise boundary between the two final outcomes.
Believers in God and His messengers have their reward and light, while deniers of signs are companions of Hell; light and the two companies meet in one ayah.
Believers are promised mercy and a light by which to walk, giving the judgment light of the right side an antecedent path function.
The oath by night as it covers begins the paired cosmic contrasts whose answer is that human striving diverges.
The oath by day as it appears supplies night's opposite before the two human courses are stated.
The oath by the creation of male and female adds another pair immediately before the declaration of divergent striving.
The oath by the sun begins a chain of paired cosmic images before the soul's two moral possibilities are disclosed.
The moon following the sun supplies the first relational counterpart in that oath chain.
Day revealing the sun begins a light-dark pair within the oath sequence.
Night covering the sun completes the light-dark pair before the soul's division.
The oath by the sky and its builder widens the ordered pairs that precede moral separation.
The oath by the earth and its spread completes the cosmic setup before the proportioned soul and its two impulses.
The most wretched person avoids the reminder, identifying the stance of the ill-fated class.
That wretched person enters the greatest Fire, turning ill fortune into destination.
In that Fire he neither dies nor lives, making the adverse destination a continuing state.
The one who purifies himself succeeds, providing the fortunate opposite to the wretched person.
The warning of a blazing Fire introduces the final outcomes of the two courses described earlier in the surah.
The person who denies and turns away is identified as the wretched one who enters that Fire.
The giver seeks no repayment of another's favor, clarifying the motive of the conduct that leads away from Fire.
Seeking only the Lord's face completes the fortunate person's stance.
The promise that he will be satisfied gives that course its final felicity.
Those who commit evil suppose they will be made like believers who do good in life and death; the verse condemns that erasure of the two outcomes.
The verse rejects making believers who do good like corrupters, or the mindful like the wicked, stating the moral boundary behind final separation.
The question rejects treating those who submit like criminals, another direct refusal to collapse the two human classes.
Everything in the heavens and earth, along with the angels, prostrates to God, completing the scene in which shadows incline on both right and left.
The one who fears receives the reminder, supplying the responsive stance immediately contrasted with the wretched person in 87:11.
Remembering the Lord's name and praying continues the successful person's course after 87:14.
Preferring the nearer life names the competing choice behind the adverse course.
The afterlife is better and more lasting, explaining why preference for the nearer life misjudges fortune.
Greedily consuming inheritance continues the conduct exposed after failure to honor the orphan and feed the needy.
Excessive love of wealth completes the earthly value system that mistakes provision for honor and leads toward the adverse judgment.
